subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: In this unit — We Are Connected — you will work through what is a network?, connect with a wire, connect without a wire, the internet: computers all around the world and online and offline (and the mini-project). Everything you need is here: explainers to read, examples to copy, things to build, practice with answers, and a project at the end. Every tool used is free and runs in a web browser.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 1 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Say that two or more computers joined together is called a network.
Know that other devices, not only computers, can join a network too (like a printer or a tablet).
Say that connected computers can share — they can talk to each other and share pictures and words.
Name devices that connect with wires — for example a printer, a desktop computer or a games console.
Name devices that connect without wires — for example a smartphone, a tablet, a laptop or a camera.
Know that the internet is lots and lots of computers joined together all around the world.
Know that when a device is joined to the internet we are online, and we can share pictures, video-call and watch videos.
Know that sometimes there is no internet (we are offline), and then some things — like an online video — will not work.

concepts.title: What is a network?
concepts.explanation: One computer on its own is just one computer. When two or more computers are joined together, we call it a network. When they are joined, they can share — they can talk to each other and share pictures and words. Other devices, like a printer, can join too. Here is one computer. and here is another computer. On their own, they cannot share. Now they are joined. They are connected. Two or more computers joined together is a network! Look — they can share!
concepts.example: Act it out with your own bodies. Ask two you to stand apart.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that joining lets you share?

concepts.title: Connect with a wire
concepts.explanation: Some computers and devices join a network with a wire. A wire is a cord that carries the sharing from one device to another. Things that often use a wire are a desktop computer, a printer and a games console. This is a wire. A wire joins two devices so they can share. Can the computer send its picture to the printer to print? Not yet — they are not joined.
concepts.example: Now there is a wire. Now the computer can send the picture to the printer, and out it comes!
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that the wire is what lets you share? Can you name one or two devices that connect with a wire?

concepts.title: Connect without a wire
concepts.explanation:
Some devices join a network with no wire at all. They join through the air. This is why you can use them in a park, on a bus, or anywhere. Devices that often need no wire are a smartphone, a tablet, a laptop and a camera.

This tablet has no wire. So how does it join? It joins through the air!
concepts.example: A phone can join with no wire — that is why you can watch it in the park or on a bus, far from any cord. Mention gently that some clever devices, like a laptop or a tablet, can join either way — with a wire or without — but they do not need to remember that.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you sort a few devices into “uses a wire” and “no wire needed”? Can you name one or two devices that connect without a wire?

concepts.title: The internet: computers all around the world
concepts.explanation: The internet is the biggest network of all. It is lots and lots of computers joined together all around the world. When your device joins the internet, you can reach people and things very, very far away — you can video-call family, share photos, and watch videos. Dot lots of little computers all around it and join them with lines. All these computers, all around the world, are joined together. That giant network is the internet. Imani lives here.
concepts.example: Her grandma lives far away in Mogadishu. Because of the internet, Imani can pick up a tablet and see Grandma's face and talk to her — even though she is so far away!
concepts.checkYourself: Can you give one thing we can do on the internet (video-call, share a photo, watch a video)?

concepts.title: Online and offline (and the Mini-Project)
concepts.explanation: When our device is joined to the internet, we are online — and online videos play, messages send, and we can share. But sometimes there is no internet. Then we are offline — the video will not play (we see a spinning circle, an animation, that means “wait” ), and a message like “No internet” may pop up. Some things still work offline, like drawing a picture or looking at photos already saved on the device. When we are joined to the internet, we are online. Watch — the video plays! But sometimes there is no internet.
concepts.example: Then we are offline. The video cannot come, so we just see a spinning circle going round and round — that is the computer saying 'please wait, I cannot find the internet.'.

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I drew two computers and a printer joined with wires.
I drew three devices that need no wire.
I told my partner why I chose them.
I answered the online or offline question.
I added one thing to make it better.
1. Two or more computers joined together is a... Tick one.
2. A printer often connects with a... Tick one.
3. Which one can connect with no wire? Tick one.

selfAssessment: I can say that two or more computers joined together is called a network.
I can know that other devices, not only computers, can join a network too (like a printer or a tablet).
I can say that connected computers can share — they can talk to each other and share pictures and words.
I can name devices that connect with wires — for example a printer, a desktop computer or a games console.
I can name devices that connect without wires — for example a smartphone, a tablet, a laptop or a camera.
I can know that the internet is lots and lots of computers joined together all around the world.
I can know that when a device is joined to the internet we are online, and we can share pictures, video-call and watch videos.
I can know that sometimes there is no internet (we are offline), and then some things — like an online video — will not work.
